title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
hookLine: he turns toward Jerusalem, and the foxes have holes

lines: IN ONE VERSE, THE BOOK TURNS.
cards: Partway through Luke's Gospel, the book turns. Until now Jesus has moved around Galilee: the lake, the villages, the hills.

Then, in one verse, he turns toward Jerusalem, the city where, as he has already told his disciples, he will suffer. From here on, Luke tells the story as one long walk. Readers call this stretch the travel narrative.
And the very first thing that happens on the road is a door shut in his face.

teach.b: Here's the hinge in the Douay-Rheims: "And it came to pass, when the days of his assumption were accomplishing, that he steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem."
Assumption here means his being taken up, to the cross and to the Father. To set your face is an old Hebrew way of speaking: fix your direction and refuse to be turned.
Isaiah's servant says he has set his face hard as rock.

teach.h: NO FIRE ON THE SAMARITAN VILLAGE.
teach.b: Jesus sends messengers ahead into a Samaritan village, and the village won't receive him, because he's headed for Jerusalem. James and John ask if they should call fire down from heaven.
Jesus rebukes them, and they simply go on to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you wherever you go.

Jesus answers: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Know what you're signing up for. The second says, let me first go and bury my father.
The third, let me first say goodbye at home.

Jesus answers with a farmer's picture: "No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." Look over your shoulder, and the furrow wanders. Luke doesn't soften these sayings.
The Church reads them not as contempt for family, which the commandments honor, but as a question of what comes first.
Jesus has set his face. He asks the people walking beside him to set theirs.

how: Catholics hear this passage at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel; the Catechism teaches that family ties matter but are not absolute, and that following Jesus comes first.

games.q: you're James. a Samaritan village has refused to welcome your teacher. what do you suggest?
o: call down fire from heaven on them.
games.why: James and John offer fire. Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they simply go on to another village.

practice: Think of one hard thing you keep circling: a conversation you keep postponing, a habit you keep almost starting, a decision you keep reopening.
Picture yourself turning your face toward it, the way you'd turn to walk a road, and notice the urge to look back without obeying it. If you pray, ask for steadiness.

wordCard.voice: assumption. Luke's word for Jesus being taken up, to the cross and to the Father, the hinge where he fixed his face toward Jerusalem. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no looking back. A hand on the plow, eyes on the furrow. Rest well.
